doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Listening to the whole band and advice to drummer students
summary: He explains why he listens to everything, urges students to study many drummers and piano, and distinguishes drummers who play drums from those who play music.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: You had said something, a comment about when musicians listen to other musicians they shouldn’t just focus on their own instrument, they should listen to the whole band to get a

sense of how it interacts. And I guess that must have paid dividends for you in that moment, because you were familiar not only with Dizzy but what his supporting sidemen were doing on those recordings.

Well that has paid big dividends in my career. Because I’m the type of drummer that always, I do a lot of listening. And I think that in my opinion, and from my experience, listening to music it is paramount. So you should listen to a lot of music, and when you listen to music, in my case I never concentrate on what the drummers were doing, I was — I listened to everything. And when I mean listened, listening, it’s not listening to an album just once. Because I have got students that I tell them you have to check Max Roach, you should check Philly Joe Jones, you should check Art Blakey, those masters that came before us, Elvin Jones, Jimmy Cobb, Billy Higgins. And they just come to me, “Oh yes I have one album with Billy Higgins with Joe Henderson.” “Oh, just one album?” So listening to a lot of music pays huge dividends and still, I’m 68, and I’m still listening to music. But use your focus, if you want to be let’s say a good drummer, an all- around drummer or a musician, you should listen and get the whole picture, know what everybody’s doing. If you can have the chance of studying the piano and learning some harmony that also is going to help. Something that I didn’t — when I was a kid I was into just playing or fooling around with my sticks, playing some rudiments and playing baseball. I didn’t pay attention to my father who told me you should study the piano, you should learn harmony. I was just into drums because I didn’t have a drumset because I was a classical music student and I wanted to play drums. So anyway my advice to students, if you’ve got good ears and when you listen to music you listen to the music as a whole and you just don’t concentrate on the lick that Max is doing, how am I going to copy this Philly Joe, how am I going to copy this Brian Blade. You’re going to be a better drummer. I have a philosophy, I always tell people there are two types of drummers in my opinion, those drummers who play the drums and those who plays music. It’s up to you. You have to decide which one you want to become. If you want to be those drummers that have a lot of incredible command of the instrument and can play all the rudiments and have a lot of chops and just concentrate on playing their instrument, or if you want to be the type of drummer who is going to play musically speaking and is going to support the band and make music. It is up to you.
